newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss bankers vow to win over U.S. critics.
newsitem.headline: Swiss bankers vow to win over U.S. critics.

text.p: Swiss bankers reacted with surprise and dismay on Friday to New York state's move to curb business ties amid a probe of Holocaust victims' dormant accounts, but vowed to win over their critics by putting facts on the table.

Banks were non-plussed by the State of New York's decision to stop placing short-term deposits in Swiss banks until it is satisfied they did not withhold deposits from Holocaust victims and their heirs, as some Jewish groups have alleged.

The step followed by one day the three biggest Swiss banks' creation of a 100 million Swiss franc ($70 million) Holocaust memorial fund as a gesture of good will that they are taking the allegations seriously but without acknowledging wrongdoing.

Wondering what more they had to do to establish their bona fides, bankers said they were eager to meet New York Banking Superintendent Neil Levin when he visits Switzerland next week, but were not about to turn over any customers' records.

"He can speak with different people, with representatives of the Banking Commission and with us, but he cannot see any documents. He does not have the authority for that," said Silvia Matile, spokeswoman for the Swiss Bankers Association.

Levin wants to review the records of Swiss Bank Corp (SBC) and Credit Suisse Group, two big banks that operated in New York during World War Two. But banks said they had already turned over any dormant accounts from the era.
"What is always overloooked is that in the state of New York all documents and money dormant for five years is turned over to the state," Matile said.
"On the other hand, it is certainly worthwhile when one can hold talks with superintendents because apparently they have not yet recognised all we have done."

SBC spokesman Michael Willi said the search for the truth about Holocaust accounts, already under way via a panel formed last May by Swiss bankers and Jewish groups, would not be served by threats to crack down on Swiss banks' U.S. operations.

"What confuses us is, we are not quite sure if the U.S. politicians really know their own laws correctly. There can be no dormant accounts in the U.S. from this time. They have to be reported to the state after five years," he added.
Willi said U.S. banking regulators had attested to SBC's correct business practices for half a century and noted that the U.S. Treasury kept a close eye on SBC during the war years.

"If Mr Levin or others say they want to review the bank's activity in New York from 1939 to 1945, they should contact the U.S. Treasury, which was in our building the whole time. No 'i' was dotted without the U.S. government knowing it," he said.

Credit Suisse Group spokesman Christoph Meier said the bank was taking New York sanctions threats seriously and was ready to cooperate with state officials. "For this reason we believe that we can put to rest any concerns," he said.

Bankers grumbled that U.S. critics were not recognising steps banks have already taken by contributing to the Holocaust fund and agreeing to work with Jewish groups to search for any dormant accounts not turned up in two prior sweeps.
"We don't quite understand what more they want from us, why they don't want to acknowledge what we have done," Matile said.
"Just what is expected from us is lacking," Willi added.
"You cannot buy yourself out of accusations. That is clear. But it would be in in the interests of the people directly involved to be able to work in peace and quiet."
Willi said SBC was taking the matter very seriously, but played down the impact if the state's move to halt deposits.
"These activities do not hit us in a vital nerve, the short-term transactions," he said.
